questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Which of these questions can be answered by doing a science test?
questions.explanation: You can measure how high a ball bounces. 'Prettiest', 'nicest' and 'best' are opinions, so people will not all agree and you cannot measure them.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Sort the questions. Can a scientist test them with measurements?
items: Which towel soaks up the most water?
Do seeds sprout faster in warm or cold places?
Does a bigger magnet pick up more paper clips?
Is Friday the best day of the week?
questions.explanation: A testable question can be answered by measuring or counting something. Questions about what is funniest, nicest or best are opinions.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: When we repeat a test and get similar results each time, the results are more ___.
questions.explanation: Repeating a measurement lets you check it. If the results are close together, you can trust them more: they are more reliable.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: A good results table has headings and units, for example 'Distance (m)'.
questions.explanation: Headings tell the reader what each column shows, and units (like m, cm or s) tell them what was measured.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: A **prediction** is…
options: what you saw happen in the test
what you think will happen, and why
a question that cannot be tested
questions.explanation: A prediction is made before the test, using what you already know. After the test, the evidence shows whether the prediction was right.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Why do scientists measure the same thing three times?
options: Because the first try is always wrong.
To make the test last longer.
To check the results and trust them more.
questions.explanation: Repeating lets you spot a result that is very different, and it makes your results more reliable. The first try is not always wrong.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Put the steps of an investigation in the right order.
sequence: Ask a question you can test.
Make a prediction.
Plan a fair test.
Measure and record the results.
Say what the evidence shows.
questions.explanation: Scientists ask, predict, plan, test and then explain. You compare the evidence with your prediction at the end.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Arif tests which type of sponge soaks up the most water. Which things must stay the same? Choose all that are right.
options: the amount of water poured on
the size of each piece of sponge
questions.explanation: In a fair test you change one thing only. Here the type of sponge is the one thing that changes. Water, size and time must be kept the same.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Force is measured in ___ and temperature in degrees ___.
questions.explanation: A forcemeter measures force in newtons (N). A thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius (°C).

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Raju tests which of two bean plants grows taller. One plant is in sunlight in a big pot. The other is in shade in a small pot. This is a fair test.
questions.explanation: Two things are different: the light and the size of the pot. If one plant grows taller, we cannot tell which change caused it. Only one thing should change.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Mina tests which kind of bean seed grows tallest. Sort each item.
questions.explanation: We change one thing (the seed), measure one thing (the height) and keep everything else the same so the test is fair.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Match each question to what you would measure to answer it.
pairs: Which cup of cha is the hottest?
How hard must we pull a box along the floor?
questions.explanation: Time is measured with a stopwatch, length with a ruler, temperature with a thermometer and force with a forcemeter.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Look at the three thermometers. What temperature does thermometer B show?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C. A reads 5 degrees, B reads 25 degrees and C reads 40 degrees.
questions.explanation: Find the top of the red liquid in thermometer B and read the scale beside it: 25 °C. Always include the unit.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Read the thermometers. Put them in order from the coldest reading to the hottest reading.
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C showing different temperatures.
sequence: Thermometer A
Thermometer B
Thermometer C
questions.explanation: A reads 12 °C, B reads 37 °C and C reads 48 °C. The higher the liquid, the higher the temperature.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Read the forcemeter. It shows a force of ___ N.
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter with its pointer at 4 newtons.
questions.explanation: The pointer is at the line marked 4, so the force is 4 newtons (4 N). Forces are measured in newtons.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Sumi drags a bag over a rough floor and reads this forcemeter. On a smooth floor the same bag needed only 4 N. How much **more** force did the rough floor need?
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter with its pointer at 7 newtons.
questions.explanation: The forcemeter reads 7 N. The difference is 7 − 4 = 3 N. A rough floor has more friction, so it needs a bigger pull.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Match each tool to the unit it uses.
questions.explanation: A thermometer uses degrees Celsius, a stopwatch uses seconds and a ruler uses centimetres.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Imran wants to find out how long a toy car takes to roll down a ramp. Which tool should he use?
questions.explanation: A stopwatch measures time in seconds. A ruler measures length and a thermometer measures temperature.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Mina wants to know which of two soaps makes more bubbles. She uses one spoonful of each soap. How should she set up the water to keep the test fair?
options: The same amount of water at the same temperature for both.
A big bowl for soap A and a small cup for soap B.
More water for the soap she thinks is better.
Warm water for soap A and cold water for soap B.
questions.explanation: Only the soap should change. If the amount or temperature of the water is different, we would not know whether the soap or the water caused the bubbles.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: A class tested how far shoes slide on a wet floor when pushed. Example results: rubber sole 10 cm, leather sole 35 cm, plastic sole 30 cm. Which shoe is the safest on a wet floor?
questions.explanation: The rubber sole slid the shortest distance, so it grips the floor best. The evidence shows it is the safest choice.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Imran times how long an ice cube takes to melt in the sun and gets 20 minutes. His friend says, 'Do it three times and see if the answers are close.' This is good advice.
questions.explanation: One result might be a mistake. Repeating the test three times lets Imran check it, and close results are more reliable.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Rafi says, 'Red toy cars roll further than blue ones.' He rolled the red car down a steep ramp and the blue car down a gentle ramp. Why is his test not fair?
questions.model_answer: He used different ramps. The ramp must be the same for both cars, so that only the colour of the car changes.
questions.explanation: The steepness of the ramp changed as well as the colour, so we cannot tell which one made the car roll further. Keep the ramp the same.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Class 3A threw paper planes. Table: newspaper 5 m, writing paper 7 m, card 3 m. In a bar chart of this table, which paper has the **tallest** bar?
questions.explanation: The height of a bar shows the size of the result. Writing paper has the biggest number (7 m), so its bar is the tallest.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Class 3C dropped three balls three times each. Example bounce heights (cm): tennis ball 40, 44, 42; rubber ball 62, 60, 64; foam ball 20, 22, 18. The **middle** result of each ball is used. Which ball had the highest middle result?
questions.explanation: Put each set in order and take the middle number. For the rubber ball: 60, 62, 64, so the middle result is 62 cm. Tennis is 42 cm and foam is 20 cm.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Imran predicts, 'The heavier the paper, the further the plane will fly.' The papers from lightest to heaviest are newspaper, writing paper, card. Example results: newspaper 5 m, writing paper 7 m, card 3 m. Does the evidence support his prediction?
options: Yes, because writing paper is heavier than newspaper and flew further.
Yes, because the heaviest paper always flies furthest.
No, because card, the heaviest paper, flew the shortest distance.
We cannot tell, because he did not draw a bar chart.
questions.explanation: If the prediction were right, card would fly furthest. It flew the shortest distance, so the evidence does not support the prediction. Scientists accept this and look for new explanations.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Arif wants to find out if the amount of water changes how tall bean seedlings grow. Which plan is the best?
options: Give four matching plants 0, 10, 20 and 30 ml a day, keeping soil, pot and light the same.
Give one plant 20 ml of water a day and measure it once.
Give four plants different amounts of water in different kinds of soil.
Water one plant a lot in the sun and another a little in the shade.
questions.explanation: Only the amount of water changes, and everything else is kept the same, so any difference in height must be caused by the water. The other plans change more than one thing or have nothing to compare.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Rafi and Mina each timed an ice cube melting three times. Rafi got 10, 11 and 10 minutes. Mina got 8, 15 and 22 minutes. Rafi's results are more reliable than Mina's.
questions.explanation: Rafi's three results are very close together, so we can trust them more. Mina's results are far apart, so she should check her method and test again.

questions.title: Science Investigators
questions.stem: Anika throws a paper plane three times and measures 5 m, 5 m and 14 m. What should she do about the 14 m result, and why?
questions.model_answer: She should check it by throwing again, because it is very different from the other two and might be a mistake.
questions.explanation: A result that is very different from the others needs checking. Repeating the throw shows whether it was a mistake or a real result.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Which of these is a job of the skeleton?
questions.explanation: The skeleton is a frame of bones that holds the body up and gives it shape. Without it we would flop like a jellyfish.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Muscles can push and pull bones.
questions.explanation: A muscle can only pull. When it contracts (gets shorter and fatter) it pulls a bone. To move the bone back, a second muscle has to pull.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Match each part of the body to its job.
pairs: pull on bones to move them
questions.explanation: Bones protect soft organs inside the body. Muscles are joined to bones and pull on them to make them move.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: When a muscle gets shorter and pulls a bone, we say that the muscle ___.
questions.explanation: A muscle contracts when it gets shorter and fatter. When it relaxes it gets longer again and stops pulling.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: A new baby has more bones than an adult has.
questions.explanation: A new baby has about 300 small bones. As the child grows, some bones join together, so an adult has 206 bones.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Why do muscles work in pairs?
options: Muscles are too heavy to work alone.
Muscles can only push, not pull.
A muscle can only pull, so another pulls back.
questions.explanation: A muscle can only pull. One muscle pulls a bone one way, and its partner pulls it back the other way.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Which of these are safe things to do with medicine? Choose all that are right.
options: Take it only when a parent, carer or doctor gives it.
Take the right amount at the right time.
Share it with a friend who feels the same way.
Take pills that look like sweets if nobody is watching.
Keep it where small children cannot reach it.
questions.explanation: Medicines can help, but they can also harm if used wrongly. Never share them, and never take medicine that looks like sweets.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how you bend your arm and then straighten it again.
sequence: The biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes.
The lower arm bone is pulled up and the arm bends.
The triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes.
The lower arm bone is pulled down and the arm is straight.
questions.explanation: To bend the arm, the biceps pulls. To straighten it, the triceps pulls and the biceps relaxes. The two muscles take turns.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Sort each example into the job it shows.
items: holding the body up so we can stand
the ribs around the heart and lungs
muscles pulling on bones to bend the arm
the biceps and triceps working as a pair
questions.explanation: Bones support the body and protect soft organs. Muscles are joined to the bones and pull them, which lets us move.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Medicines are drugs that help us when we are ___.
questions.explanation: Medicines can stop pain, fight infections or help the body heal when we are ill. They must be used carefully.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: About how many bones does an adult human have?
questions.explanation: An adult has 206 bones. A baby has about 300 small bones, but some of them join together as the child grows.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: What happens to your bones as you grow up?
questions.explanation: Bones grow longer and stronger as you grow, which is why you get taller.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Look at the skeleton. Which number shows the bone that protects the brain?
questions.image_alt: A human skeleton with six bones numbered 1 to 6.
questions.explanation: Number 1 is the skull. It is a hard case that protects the soft brain. Number 2 is the ribs, which protect the heart and lungs.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Number 3 on the skeleton is the ___.
questions.image_alt: A human skeleton with six bones numbered 1 to 6.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is the spine, also called the backbone. It holds the body up and protects the spinal cord.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Look at the arm. Which number is the muscle that contracts to bend the arm?
questions.image_alt: An arm showing a bone, the biceps, the triceps and the elbow joint, numbered 1 to 4.
questions.explanation: Number 2 is the biceps. It contracts, gets shorter and pulls the lower arm up. Number 3, the triceps, relaxes at the same time.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Number 3 in the picture is the triceps. It relaxes when you bend your arm.
questions.image_alt: An arm showing a bone, the biceps, the triceps and the elbow joint, numbered 1 to 4.
questions.explanation: The triceps and biceps work as a pair. When the biceps (number 2) contracts to bend the arm, the triceps relaxes.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Match each picture to the way it helps keep the body healthy.
questions.explanation: Eating well, washing hands, exercising and sleeping all help to keep us healthy. Milk gives calcium, which bones need to grow strong.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Which animals have a bony skeleton inside their bodies? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: Dogs, birds, fish and frogs all have bones inside their bodies. Jellyfish and worms have soft bodies with no bones.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Mina wants strong bones. Which food should she choose?
questions.explanation: Bones need calcium to grow strong. Milk, yoghurt, green leafy vegetables and small fish give calcium. Sweets and doughnuts do not.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Mina has a cough. She finds a bottle of syrup that her sister used last week. What should she do?
options: Take a big spoonful so it works faster.
Ask a parent or carer before taking any.
Give some to her friend who also coughs.
Take a little every hour until she feels better.
questions.explanation: Only take medicine that a parent, carer or doctor gives you, in the right amount. Medicine that was right for someone else may not be right for you.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Families in Bangladesh often eat tiny fish such as mola whole. Why are they good for children's bones?
options: They are small enough to fit in a bowl.
They swim fast, so they are very strong.
They have no bones, so they are soft to eat.
Their bones are eaten too and contain calcium.
questions.explanation: Mola are eaten whole, bones and all. Fish bones contain calcium, which children need to build strong bones.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Moung rides his bicycle to school. What protects his head best if he falls?
questions.explanation: A helmet is hard and padded. It protects the skull, which protects the brain inside. A cap, scarf or raincoat would not.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Anika's little brother has a fever. She gives him some of her own medicine from the cupboard. This is a safe thing to do.
questions.explanation: Medicine should only be given by a parent, carer or doctor, in the right amount. Never share medicines, because they can harm someone if used wrongly.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Nadia's family keeps all the medicines on a high shelf. Explain why.
questions.model_answer: Small children cannot reach them, so they cannot take them by mistake. Medicines can be harmful if they are used wrongly.
questions.explanation: Medicines help when used the right way, but they can be dangerous if a small child takes them by mistake. Keeping them high up keeps children safe.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Class 3B measured arm length and bean-bag throw (example data): Ana 48 cm, 8 m; Bilu 52 cm, 10 m; Chandni 50 cm, 7 m; Dipu 55 cm, 11 m; Eva 46 cm, 9 m. Which statement matches the data?
options: Eva has the shortest arms but threw further than Chandni.
questions.explanation: Eva (46 cm) threw 9 m but Chandni (50 cm) threw only 7 m, so longer arms do not always throw further. Strength and practice matter too.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: Rafi says, 'I straighten my arm by pushing with my biceps.' What is wrong with this idea?
options: Arms straighten without using any muscle.
The biceps is a bone, not a muscle.
Muscles only pull: the triceps pulls the arm straight.
The biceps pulls harder when it relaxes.
questions.explanation: A muscle can only pull, never push. To straighten the arm the triceps contracts and pulls, while the biceps relaxes.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: An earthworm has no bones. Why can it not stand up tall like a dog?
questions.model_answer: A worm has no skeleton to hold its soft body up, so its body flops over.
questions.explanation: A skeleton supports the body and holds it up. Without bones, a worm's soft body cannot stand up on its own.

questions.title: Skeletons, Muscles and Medicines
questions.stem: A child needs 3 glasses of milk a day for strong bones. In 2 weeks she misses 4 glasses in total. She drinks ___ glasses.
questions.explanation: Two weeks is 14 days, and 3 × 14 = 42 glasses. She misses 4, so 42 − 4 = 38 glasses.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Which of these plants grows flowers that make seeds?
questions.explanation: A mango tree is a flowering plant. Ferns and mosses have no flowers, and pine trees make their seeds in cones.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Sort these plants into flowering and non-flowering.
questions.explanation: Rice, lotus and mango trees grow flowers that make seeds. Ferns and mosses grow from tiny spores, and pine trees make seeds in cones.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: When a seed starts to grow, we say that it ___.
questions.explanation: Germination is the start of a seed's growth. A seed needs water and warmth to germinate.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Which plant makes its seeds in cones instead of in flowers?
questions.explanation: Pine trees are non-flowering plants that make seeds in cones. Ferns do not make seeds at all: they grow from tiny spores.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Ferns grow flowers that make seeds.
questions.explanation: Ferns have no flowers. They grow from tiny parts called spores.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Match each stage of a plant's life to what it is.
pairs: can germinate when it has water and warmth
a young plant with its first leaves
a fully grown plant that makes flowers
questions.explanation: A plant goes from seed to seedling to mature plant. The mature plant makes flowers, and then fruits with new seeds.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Which is the best way to measure how tall a bean plant is each week?
questions.explanation: A ruler measures height in centimetres, so you can compare the weeks fairly. Guessing is not accurate.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Which of these are good ways to measure a plant's growth? Choose all that are right.
options: measure its height with a ruler
measure the width of its stem
count the clouds in the sky
questions.explanation: We can measure height, count leaves or measure the width of the stem each week. Clouds and smells do not tell us how much the plant has grown.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Sort these life-cycle stages into the right life cycle.
questions.explanation: A plant starts as a seed, becomes a seedling and then an adult plant with flowers. A chicken starts as an egg, hatches as a chick and grows into a hen.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: A bean seed kept dry in a packet will germinate.
questions.explanation: A seed needs water and warmth to germinate. Dry seeds in a packet can stay as seeds for a long time.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: A young plant is called a ___, and a young chicken is called a ___.
questions.explanation: A seedling is the young stage of a plant, like a chick is the young stage of a chicken.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Example: a mango seedling is 12 cm tall. Two weeks later it is 19 cm tall. It has grown ___ cm.
questions.explanation: To find how much it grew, subtract the first height from the second: 19 − 12 = 7 cm.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Look at the plant. Which number shows the roots?
questions.image_alt: A plant with five parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Number 4 is the roots, under the ground. Number 2 is a leaf, 3 is the stem and 5 is the fruit.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Number 5 holds the new seeds. It is the ___.
questions.image_alt: A plant with five parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Number 5 is the fruit. After the flower is pollinated, seeds grow inside the fruit.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Put the stages of a flowering plant's life cycle in order, starting from the seed.
questions.image_alt: The life cycle of a flowering plant with seven stages numbered 1 to 7.
sequence: seed
germination
young plant
flowering
pollination
fertilisation and fruit
seed dispersal
questions.explanation: A seed germinates and grows into a young plant, which flowers. After pollination, fruit and seeds form, and the seeds are spread so the cycle can start again.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Insects or the wind carry pollen from flower to flower. Which number on the life cycle shows this stage?
questions.image_alt: The life cycle of a flowering plant with seven stages numbered 1 to 7.
questions.explanation: Number 5 is pollination. Number 4 is the flowering stage before it, and number 7 is seed dispersal, when the seeds are spread.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: A seedling is a young plant. Which stage in the chicken's life cycle is the same kind of stage?
questions.image_alt: The life cycle of a chicken: egg, hatching, chick and adult hen.
questions.explanation: A chick is a young chicken, just as a seedling is a young plant. The egg is more like the seed, and the hen is like the adult plant.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Which picture shows a seedling, a young plant with its first leaves?
questions.explanation: A seedling is small, with just a stem and its first leaves. The sunflower and the tree are fully grown plants.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Abdul is a rice farmer in Mymensingh. Put his year in the right order.
sequence: He soaks rice seeds in water so they germinate.
He grows the seedlings in a small bed of mud.
He moves the seedlings to the big flooded field.
The rice plants flower and the grains grow.
He harvests the golden grains.
questions.explanation: Rice goes through the whole life cycle in about four months: seed, seedling, mature plant with flowers, and new seeds (the grains). Abdul keeps some seeds to plant next year.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Priya wants her bean seeds to germinate. What should she do?
options: Keep them dry in a warm cupboard.
Put them in damp soil in a freezer.
Leave them in a dry packet in the cold.
Plant them in damp soil in a warm place.
questions.explanation: Seeds need both water and warmth to germinate. Each of the other choices leaves out water or warmth.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Tuli measures her chilli plant with a ruler each week and writes the height in a table. This is a good way to see how fast it grows.
questions.explanation: Measuring at the same time each week and recording the numbers lets her compare the heights and see the growth pattern.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: On a school walk, Anika finds a plant with feathery leaves. It has no flowers and grows from tiny spores. Which plant is it most likely to be?
questions.explanation: Ferns and mosses have no flowers and grow from spores. Sunflowers, mango trees and rice are flowering plants.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: A mango tree makes many fruits, each with a seed, but only a few of the seeds grow into new trees. Why do plants make so many seeds?
questions.model_answer: Many seeds are eaten by animals or land in places where they cannot grow, so making lots of seeds means that some will grow into new plants.
questions.explanation: Many seeds never become plants because they are eaten or land somewhere unsuitable. By making lots of seeds, the plant makes sure that some survive.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Class 3C measured a bean plant. Example heights: week 1 = 2 cm, week 2 = 6 cm, week 3 = 11 cm, week 4 = 17 cm, week 5 = 20 cm. Between which two weeks did it grow the **most**?
questions.explanation: The growth was 4 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm and 3 cm. The biggest jump was between weeks 3 and 4: 17 − 11 = 6 cm. The tallest plant is not the same as the biggest growth.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: The bean plant (example data) was 2, 6, 11, 17 and 20 cm tall in weeks 1 to 5. Which prediction for week 6 fits the pattern best?
options: about 35 cm: it grows faster every week
about 22 cm: the growth is slowing down
questions.explanation: The weekly growth went 4, 5, 6 and then only 3 cm, so growth is slowing. Adding a little more to 20 cm gives about 22 cm.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Class 3B tested bean seeds (example). A: damp cotton wool in a warm room, 9 of 10 seeds germinated. B: damp cotton wool in a cold fridge, 0 germinated. C: dry cotton wool in a warm room, 0 germinated. What does the test show that seeds need to germinate?
questions.model_answer: Seeds need both water and warmth to germinate. The seeds that were cold or dry did not grow.
questions.explanation: Only seeds that were damp and warm germinated. B was damp but cold, and C was warm but dry, and neither germinated, so seeds need both water and warmth.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: Which statements are true for both a bean plant and a chicken? Choose all that are right.
options: They start life small and grow into adults.
They make new young that start the cycle again.
They begin life as a seed.
questions.explanation: Both have a life cycle with young and adult stages, and adults make new young. But only the plant starts as a seed, and only the chicken lays eggs.

questions.title: Plant Growth and Development
questions.stem: A bean plant was 2, 6, 11, 17 and 20 cm tall in weeks 1 to 5 (example data). It grew by the same number of centimetres every week.
questions.explanation: It grew 4, 5, 6 and then 3 cm. The amounts are different each week, so the growth was not steady.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: A **habitat** is…
options: a body part that helps an animal survive
the place where a living thing lives
questions.explanation: A habitat is the place where an animal or plant lives. It gives food, water, shelter and a safe place to raise young.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Match each animal to the body part or feature that suits its home.
questions.explanation: Each animal has body parts that help it live in its habitat. This is called adaptation.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: A body part or behaviour that helps an animal survive in its habitat is called an ___.
questions.explanation: Adaptations, like gills or webbed feet, help animals live in the place where they are found.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Which adaptations help a fish live in water?
questions.explanation: Gills let a fish breathe under water, and fins help it swim. A hump suits a camel, and long arms suit a monkey.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Sort each body part by the animal that has it.
items: wide feet for walking on sand
questions.explanation: Fish live in water, camels live in hot deserts and monkeys live in trees. Each has body parts that suit its habitat.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: A habitat gives an animal food, water and shelter.
questions.explanation: A good habitat gives an animal everything it needs, including a safe place to raise its young.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Which animals change their surroundings to meet their needs? Choose all that are right.
options: a baya weaver bird weaving a hanging nest
termites building a tall mud mound
an earthworm digging tunnels in soil
a fish swimming in a river
questions.explanation: Weaver birds, termites and earthworms all change the place where they live. Swimming and walking do not change the habitat.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Termites build tall mounds of ___, and earthworms dig ___ in the soil.
questions.explanation: Termites build mounds from mud, and earthworms make tunnels as they move through the soil.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Put the steps of the woodlice investigation in a sensible order.
sequence: Put 10 woodlice in a tray with one dark, damp end and one light, dry end.
Wait for 10 minutes.
Count the woodlice at each end.
Draw a bar chart of the results.
Gently return the woodlice to where you found them.
questions.explanation: Set up the test, wait, count and show the results. Woodlice are living things, so we always return them safely to their habitat.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: A key asks yes/no questions to help you name a living thing.
questions.explanation: You start at the top of the key and follow the answers, one yes/no question at a time, until you reach the name.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: A monkey is suited to living in ___, because it has long arms and a tail for climbing.
questions.explanation: Long arms and a tail help a monkey climb and swing through the trees where it finds food and shelter.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Why could a fish not live in a tree?
questions.model_answer: A fish needs water. It has gills to breathe in water and fins to swim, so it could not breathe or move in a tree.
questions.explanation: A fish's body is suited to water, not to air. Without water it could not breathe with its gills.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Why is an earthworm's thin, slimy body useful?
options: It helps the worm slide through the soil.
It helps the worm climb trees.
It helps the worm fly away from danger.
It helps the worm swim fast in the sea.
questions.explanation: A thin, slimy body slides easily between soil particles. This adaptation suits the earthworm's habitat.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Look at the pond. Which number shows the animal that breathes under water with gills?
questions.image_alt: A pond ecosystem with the Sun, air, a duck, a fish, water, a rock, water plants and a frog, numbered 1 to 8.
questions.explanation: Number 4 is the fish, which breathes with gills. Number 3 is a duck, 7 is water plants and 8 is a frog.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Look at the pond habitat. Which numbers show animals? Choose all that are right.
questions.image_alt: A pond ecosystem with the Sun, air, a duck, a fish, water, a rock, water plants and a frog, numbered 1 to 8.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is a duck, 4 is a fish and 8 is a frog. Number 5 is water and 6 is a rock, which are not living things.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Match each animal to its habitat.
questions.explanation: Each animal lives where its body is suited: monkeys climb trees, fish swim, worms burrow and camels cope with heat and sand.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Sort the animals by where they live.
questions.explanation: Fish and ducks live on or in water, monkeys and many birds live in trees, and earthworms live in the soil.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Which animal is best suited to living in a hot desert?
questions.explanation: A camel stores fat in its hump and has wide feet that do not sink in sand. A polar bear lives in the cold, and a fish needs water.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Use this key. Q1: Does it have legs? Yes: go to Q2. No: go to Q3. Q2: Does it have feathers? Yes: bird. No: cow. Q3: Does it live in water? Yes: fish. No: snake. Sumi's animal has no legs and does not live in water. Which animal is it?
questions.explanation: No legs sends you to Q3. 'Does it live in water?' is No, so the answer is snake.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: A pond is dug in a school garden in Sylhet. A few weeks later frogs, water insects and a duck arrive. Why did the animals come?
options: It gives them water, food and shelter.
It gives them tall trees to climb.
questions.explanation: A habitat gives animals food, water and shelter. The new pond became a habitat for animals that are suited to living in or near water.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: In the Sundarbans, fiddler crabs dig holes in the mud. What do the holes do for the crabs when the tide comes in?
options: help them make the water salty
questions.explanation: The crabs dig holes in the mud to hide when the tide comes in. This is an animal changing its surroundings to meet its needs.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: The baya weaver bird weaves a nest that hangs from the tip of a branch, often over water. The door is at the bottom of a long tube. How does this keep the eggs safe?
questions.model_answer: Snakes and big birds find it very hard to reach the eggs, because the nest hangs from a thin branch and the entrance is at the end of a long tube.
questions.explanation: The weaver changes its habitat to make a safe home. Enemies such as snakes cannot easily climb along the branch or up the tube to the eggs.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: If a forest is cut down, the monkeys that live there lose their food and shelter.
questions.explanation: Forest trees give monkeys food and a safe place to live. Without them the monkeys may have to move away, and some may die.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Joy wants to find some woodlice in her garden in Dhaka. Where is she most likely to find them?
options: under a damp stone in a shady corner
in the middle of a bright, dry path
questions.explanation: Woodlice prefer dark, damp places. In the class test, 9 of 10 woodlice moved to the dark, damp end of the tray.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: In a tray, 9 of 10 woodlice moved to the dark, damp end and 1 to the light, dry end. Rafi says, 'This proves that woodlice like darkness.' What is wrong with his claim?
options: The dark end was also damp, so we cannot tell if they chose the dark or the damp.
Woodlice cannot choose where to go.
The test needs 100 woodlice before it proves anything.
questions.explanation: Two things were different at each end: light and dampness. To test darkness alone, both ends should be equally damp and only the light should change.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Mina wants a key to sort a bird, a snake, a cow and a fish. Which first question splits them into two groups of two?
questions.explanation: Bird and cow have legs; snake and fish do not. 'Feathers' and 'water' each pick out just one animal, and every one of them is an animal.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Class 3A wants to find out if woodlice prefer dark or light, not damp or dry. Which changes would make the test better? Choose all that are right.
options: Make both ends of the tray equally damp.
Make one end dark and the other end light.
Put the damp paper at the dark end only.
questions.explanation: Only the light should change, so the dampness must be the same at both ends. Repeating the test makes the results more reliable. One woodlouse is not enough evidence.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.stem: Which of these is an animal **changing its habitat**, rather than a body part that suits it?
questions.explanation: Wide feet, gills and long arms are adaptations of the body. A termite mound is something the animal builds, so it changes its surroundings.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: An **ecosystem** is…
options: a group of animals of the same kind
living and non-living things together in a place, depending on each other
a place where only plants live
questions.explanation: An ecosystem includes plants, animals and microbes together with non-living things such as water, soil, rocks, air and sunlight. They all depend on each other.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Sort the parts of a school garden into living and non-living.
questions.explanation: Plants and animals are living things. Sunlight, soil, rocks and air are non-living, but living things need them.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: An ecosystem has living things and ___ things such as water, soil and sunlight.
questions.explanation: Water, soil, rocks, air and sunlight are the non-living parts of an ecosystem.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Sunlight is a living part of an ecosystem.
questions.explanation: Sunlight is non-living. Living things need it, but it is not alive itself.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Sort these ecosystems into aquatic (in water) and terrestrial (on land).
questions.explanation: Coral reefs, streams and sea grass beds are in water. Grasslands and forests are on land.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Where in Bangladesh can you find a coral reef?
questions.explanation: Saint Martin's Island is the only coral island in Bangladesh. Corals, colourful fish, sea snails and turtles live around it.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Which living things might you find in a hill stream? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Small fish, crabs, insects and water plants live in streams. Coral and sea turtles live in the sea.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Aquatic means living in ___, and terrestrial means living on ___.
questions.explanation: Aquatic ecosystems are in water, such as ponds, streams and the sea. Terrestrial ecosystems are on land, such as forests and grasslands.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Which non-living things help to decide which plants and animals can live in a place? Choose all that are right.
options: the amount of light and heat
whether the water is salty or fresh
the colour of the sky at night
questions.explanation: Water, light, heat, soil and saltiness all decide which living things can survive. The colour of the night sky makes no difference to where plants and animals live.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: A water lily could grow well in a dry field.
questions.explanation: Water lilies need fresh water and sunlight. A dry field has no water for them.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Put the steps of the 'sunny or shady' plant investigation in order.
sequence: Choose a sunny place and a shady place under a tree.
Lay a 1 metre square of string on the ground in each place.
Count the plants inside each square.
Draw a bar chart of the numbers.
Say where more plants grew, and why.
questions.explanation: Use the same size square in both places so the test is fair, then count, show the results in a chart and explain what they show.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Only special trees can grow in the salty mud of the ___, home of the tiger.
questions.explanation: The Sundarbans is a mangrove ecosystem. Sundari trees and other special trees can live in its salty mud.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Sort these living things by the ecosystem where they live.
questions.explanation: Each ecosystem has its own plants and animals, suited to its water, soil and light.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Look at the pond. Which numbers show non-living things? Choose all that are right.
questions.image_alt: A pond ecosystem with the Sun, air, a duck, a fish, water, a rock, water plants and a frog, numbered 1 to 8.
questions.explanation: Number 1 is the Sun, 5 is water and 6 is a rock, so they are non-living. Number 3 is a duck and 7 is water plants, which are living.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Look at the pond. Which number shows a living thing that is **not** an animal?
questions.image_alt: A pond ecosystem with the Sun, air, a duck, a fish, water, a rock, water plants and a frog, numbered 1 to 8.
questions.explanation: Number 7 is water plants: they are living but they are not animals. Number 2 is air and clouds, 5 is water and 6 is a rock, so they are non-living.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Sort the pictures of a pond into living and non-living.
questions.explanation: Fish, frogs, ducks and water lilies are living things. Water, stones and sunlight are non-living parts of the pond ecosystem.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Match each picture to the ecosystem where it lives.
questions.explanation: Tigers live in the Sundarbans mangrove, corals build reefs in the sea, water lilies grow in wetlands, and cattle graze on grassland.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Look at the mangrove tree. What kind of mud and water does it grow in?
questions.image_alt: A mangrove tree with breathing roots and prop roots standing in salty mud and salty water.
questions.explanation: Mangrove trees grow in salty mud and salty water. Most other trees cannot live in such salty places.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Which animal lives in the Sundarbans mangrove forest?
questions.explanation: Tigers, deer, crabs and crocodiles live in the Sundarbans. Penguins live in cold places and camels in deserts.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Moung lives near a haor in Sunamganj. For much of the year the land is covered with water. Which ecosystem is this?
questions.explanation: A wetland is land covered with water for much of the year. Haors and beels in Sylhet and Sunamganj are wetlands with water lilies, fish, ducks and frogs.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Joy visits Saint Martin's Island and sees a piece of coral. What is the best thing to do?
options: Break off a small piece to take home.
Walk on the coral to get a good photo.
Pick it up and carry it to the boat.
Look at it without touching or breaking it.
questions.explanation: Corals are tiny animals that build hard homes that grow very slowly. Walking on or breaking coral harms the reef, so we look but do not touch.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Rafi's school pond dries up in a very hot, dry season. The fish and water lilies that lived in it cannot live there any more.
questions.explanation: Fish and water lilies need water. Without it the pond is no longer a suitable habitat for them.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Class 3B counted 32 plants in a sunny square and 12 in a shady square. Which non-living thing most likely explains why more plants grew in the sunny square?
questions.explanation: Plants need light to make their food. The sunny square got more light, so more plants could grow there.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Write one rule for tourists visiting the coral reef at Saint Martin's Island, and say why it matters.
questions.model_answer: Do not touch or break the coral, because corals are living animals that grow very slowly and can be harmed.
questions.explanation: Tourists can harm the reef by walking on coral, breaking pieces off or leaving plastic rubbish. Clear rules protect this special ecosystem.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Tuli counts the plants in a 1 m square in a sunny place and in a 2 m square in a shady place. Why is her test not fair?
options: The two squares are different sizes.
A metre is too short to measure.
She should count animals as well.
questions.explanation: A bigger square will usually hold more plants. To compare sun and shade fairly, both squares must be the same size, so only the amount of light changes.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: In a 1 m square of sunny ground there were 32 plants (example data). About how many plants would you expect in 2 square metres of the same sunny ground, if the plants are spread out evenly?
questions.explanation: Two squares of the same size hold twice as many plants: 32 + 32 = 64.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: A scientist wants to grow corals and water lilies in the same tank. Why will this not work?
options: Corals need salty water but water lilies need fresh water.
Corals and water lilies eat each other.
Water lilies are animals and corals are plants.
Corals need fresh water and sunlight.
questions.explanation: The non-living features decide who can live where. Coral needs warm, clear, salty water, but water lilies need fresh water and sunlight.

questions.title: Ecosystems of Bangladesh
questions.stem: A pond ecosystem dries up in a very dry season. What will happen to the living things in it, and why?
questions.model_answer: The water is gone, so the fish, frogs and water plants cannot live there. They will die or the animals will move away.
questions.explanation: Water is a very important non-living part of a pond ecosystem. When it disappears, the living things lose their home and their water.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Every food chain starts with a…
questions.explanation: Producers are green plants. They make their own food using sunlight, water and air, so every food chain begins with one.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Sort these living things into producers, consumers and decomposers.
questions.explanation: Plants make their own food. Animals eat living plants or animals. Mushrooms, moulds and worms break down dead things.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: In a food chain, the arrows point from the ___ to the animal that eats it.
blanks: plant or animal that is eaten
questions.explanation: An arrow means 'is eaten by'. So grass → goat shows that the goat eats the grass.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: makes its own food using sunlight
breaks down dead things into the soil
questions.explanation: A predator hunts prey. A tiger is a consumer and a predator, and the deer it hunts is its prey.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Animals can make their own food using sunlight.
questions.explanation: Only green plants make their own food from sunlight. Animals are consumers: they must eat plants or other animals.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Why are decomposers important?
options: They hunt other animals so the predators have less food.
They make food from sunlight for every animal in the chain.
They break dead things down into goodness for the soil.
They stop plants and animals from ever dying.
questions.explanation: Decomposers recycle dead plants and animals into goodness in the soil, which helps new plants grow. Without them dead leaves and animals would pile up everywhere.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Put this rice-field food chain in order, starting with the producer.
sequence: grass
grasshopper
frog
snake
questions.explanation: The grasshopper eats the grass, the frog eats the grasshopper and the snake eats the frog. The arrows point along the chain.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Which of these are decomposers? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Mushrooms and moulds (fungi) and earthworms break down dead things. Grass is a producer and tigers are consumers.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Without ___, dead leaves and animals would pile up everywhere.
questions.explanation: Decomposers such as worms, mushrooms and microbes break down dead things so that their goodness can return to the soil.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: If the predators of an animal disappear, the number of that animal often goes up.
questions.explanation: With fewer predators to eat them, more of the prey animals survive. This pattern helps us predict what happens in a food chain.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, all the frogs are caught and sold. What happens to the grasshoppers and to the snakes?
questions.model_answer: There will be more grasshoppers because no frogs eat them, and the snakes will have less food.
questions.explanation: No frogs means fewer predators for the grasshoppers, so their number rises. The snakes lose their food, so there will be fewer of them.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Where does the energy in a food chain first come from?
questions.explanation: Producers use sunlight to make their own food. Consumers get that energy when they eat the plants, or eat animals that ate the plants.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Decomposers turn dead things back into goodness in the ___, which helps new plants grow.
questions.explanation: Decomposers recycle what was once living. The goodness they add to the soil is used by new plants.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Look at the food chain. Which living thing is the **producer**?
questions.image_alt: A food chain in a rice field: grass, then grasshopper, then frog, then snake.
questions.explanation: Grass is a green plant that makes its own food using sunlight, so it is the producer. The other three are consumers.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Look at the food chain. Which of these are consumers? Choose all that are right.
questions.image_alt: A food chain in a rice field: grass, then grasshopper, then frog, then snake.
questions.explanation: The grasshopper, frog and snake are animals that eat other living things, so they are consumers. Grass is the producer.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Look at the Sundarbans food chain. What does the arrow from the deer to the tiger mean?
questions.image_alt: A food chain in the Sundarbans: leaves, then deer, then tiger.
options: The tiger is bigger than the deer.
questions.explanation: An arrow points from the food to the animal that eats it. So the arrow from the deer to the tiger means that the tiger eats the deer.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Use the pictures to build a food chain. Start with the producer.
questions.explanation: Leaves are the producer. The caterpillar eats the leaves and the bird eats the caterpillar: leaves → caterpillar → bird.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Sort the pictures by the job each living thing does.
questions.explanation: Plants are producers, animals that eat are consumers, and mushrooms and worms are decomposers.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Match each animal to its food.
questions.explanation: A goat eats grass, a frog eats grasshoppers and a tiger eats deer. Each pair is one link in a food chain.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: In a rice field, people catch and sell most of the frogs. What is likely to happen to the insects that eat the rice?
questions.explanation: Frogs eat insects. With fewer frogs, more insects survive and they eat more of the rice. That is why many farmers now protect frogs.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Class 3C kept three slices of bread in bags (example results). Dry bread: no mould after 7 days. Damp bread in a warm room: mould after 3 days. Damp bread in the fridge: mould after 7 days. Which bread went mouldy first?
options: the damp bread in the warm room
the damp bread in the fridge
the dry bread in the bag
the three slices all at the same time
questions.explanation: Mould is a decomposer that grows best where it is damp and warm. The damp slice in the warm room went mouldy after only 3 days.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Class 3C finds a bag with mouldy bread. To check it, they open the bag and smell the bread.
questions.explanation: Never open the bag or smell mouldy bread. Mould can make you ill. Throw the bags away sealed and wash your hands.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Mina puts fruit peels and fallen leaves in a heap in the garden. After some weeks the heap has become dark, crumbly soil. Which living things did this work?
options: goats that eat the fruit peels
snakes that hunt in the heap
grass that grows on the heap
questions.explanation: Worms, moulds and microbes are decomposers. They break down the peels and leaves into goodness for the soil.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Frogs live in many rice fields in Bangladesh. How can frogs help rice farmers?
questions.model_answer: Frogs eat the insects that damage the rice, so farmers need to use less poison on their crops.
questions.explanation: Frogs are predators of insects that damage rice. When farmers protect the frogs, they need fewer pesticides.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: In a rice field the chain is grass → grasshopper → frog → snake. A farmer sprays poison that kills most of the grasshoppers. What is most likely to happen next?
options: Frogs and snakes will have less to eat.
The snakes will start eating the grass.
The frogs will find more food than before.
Nothing will change for frogs or snakes.
questions.explanation: Fewer grasshoppers means less food for the frogs, and fewer frogs means less food for the snakes. A change at one link affects the whole chain.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: In the Sundarbans chain leaves → deer → tiger, the number of deer falls a lot. Which prediction is the best?
options: Tigers will have more food, so there will be more tigers.
The leaves will disappear because deer protect them.
Tigers will have less food, and more leaves will be left.
Nothing will change because tigers can eat leaves.
questions.explanation: Fewer deer eat fewer leaves, so more leaves are left. Tigers eat deer, so they will have less food. Predators suffer when their prey becomes scarce.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: If all the decomposers in a forest died, dead leaves and animals would pile up and less goodness would return to the soil for new plants.
questions.explanation: Decomposers recycle dead things into goodness in the soil. Without them, dead material piles up and plants would have less goodness to grow with.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy Roles
questions.stem: Class 3C bread results (example): dry bread, no mould after 7 days; damp bread in a warm room, mould after 3 days; damp bread in the fridge, mould after 7 days. Which statements does the evidence support? Choose all that are right.
options: Mould grew faster on damp bread than on dry bread.
Mould grew faster in the warm room than in the fridge.
Mould only ever grows on dry bread.
Bread in a fridge can never go mouldy.
questions.explanation: Both damp slices went mouldy, but the dry one did not, so damp helps mould. The warm slice went mouldy sooner than the fridge slice. The fridge slice did go mouldy after 7 days.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how we see the Moon shine at night.
sequence: The Sun shines light on the Moon.
The light hits the Moon's surface.
The light bounces (reflects) off the Moon.
The light reaches our eyes.
We see the Moon shining.
questions.explanation: The Moon has no light of its own. It reflects sunlight, and the reflected light travels to our eyes.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Match each space object to what it is.
pairs: a ball of hot glowing gas
a space rock that burns up in our air
questions.explanation: A star makes its own light. A planet orbits a star and a moon orbits a planet. A meteor is a "shooting star" and a satellite can send signals to us.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Put the first six planets in order, starting nearest the Sun.
sequence: Mercury
Venus
Earth
Mars
Jupiter
Saturn
questions.explanation: The order from the Sun is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. "My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming" helps you remember.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: The Moon makes its own light.
questions.explanation: The Moon only looks bright because it reflects light from the Sun. The Sun is a star and makes its own light.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: The Earth takes one ___ to go once around the ___.
questions.explanation: The Earth orbits the Sun once in a year. The Moon orbits the Earth.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: What keeps the planets going around the Sun?
questions.explanation: The Sun's gravity pulls on the planets and keeps them in their paths (orbits).

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Which of these are planets in our solar system? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Mars, Jupiter and Saturn are planets. The Sun is a star and the Moon is a moon that orbits the Earth.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Sort each object into star, planet or moon.
items: one of the four moons Galileo saw near Jupiter
questions.explanation: Stars make their own light. Planets travel around a star, and moons travel around a planet.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Match each scientist to what they discovered or said.
pairs: said the planets go around the Sun
wrote about how the universe began
questions.explanation: Aryabhata said the Earth spins, Copernicus put the Sun at the centre, Galileo used a telescope to find Jupiter's moons, and Dr Jamal Nazrul Islam of Chattogram studied the universe.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Why does the Moon shine at night if it has no light of its own?
questions.model_answer: Sunlight bounces off (reflects from) the Moon and reaches our eyes.
questions.explanation: We see the Moon because it reflects the Sun's light, just like a mirror reflects a torch beam.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Earth is the only planet we know that has living things.
questions.explanation: Earth has water, air and the right temperature for life. Scientists have not found living things on any other planet yet.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: A meteor, or "shooting star", is really a…
options: star that has fallen to Earth
space rock burning up in our air
questions.explanation: A meteor is a small space rock that burns up as it hurtles through the air around Earth, making a bright streak. It is not a real star.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: An artificial satellite is a machine that people send into space to orbit a planet.
questions.explanation: People build artificial satellites for TV, phones and weather. Bangabandhu Satellite-1 orbits the Earth and is Bangladesh's first.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Look at the planets in order from the Sun. Which number is the Earth?
questions.image_alt: The Sun and eight planets in a row, numbered 1 to 8 from the Sun (not to scale).
questions.explanation: Earth is the third planet from the Sun, after Mercury (1) and Venus (2). Mars is number 4.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Which number is Jupiter, the biggest planet?
questions.image_alt: The Sun and eight planets in a row, numbered 1 to 8 from the Sun (not to scale).
questions.explanation: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the biggest planet in the solar system. Saturn (6) comes next.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Match each number in the picture to its planet.
questions.image_alt: The Sun and eight planets in a row, numbered 1 to 8 from the Sun (not to scale).
questions.explanation: Counting out from the Sun: 1 Mercury, 2 Venus, 3 Earth, 4 Mars, 5 Jupiter, 6 Saturn, 7 Uranus, 8 Neptune.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: In the picture, number 4 is Mars. Mars is nearer to the Sun than Earth is.
questions.image_alt: The Sun and eight planets in a row, numbered 1 to 8 from the Sun (not to scale).
questions.explanation: Earth is number 3 and Mars is number 4, so Mars is further from the Sun than Earth.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Match each picture to what it is.
questions.explanation: The Sun is a star. Saturn is a planet with rings. The Moon travels around the Earth, a meteor streaks across the sky, and a satellite is a machine that orbits.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Moung wants to see the Sun better, so he plans to look at it through dark sunglasses. What is the right advice?
options: It is safe for a minute.
questions.explanation: Never look at the Sun, even through sunglasses or a telescope. It can damage your eyes.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Nadia's family lives on an island where it is hard to lay cables. How can they get TV and internet?
options: by signals from the Moon's light
questions.explanation: A satellite such as Bangabandhu Satellite-1 sends TV and internet signals across Bangladesh, even to islands and hills.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: A weather satellite sees a cyclone forming over the Bay of Bengal. How does this help people on the coast?
options: It warns them early so they can reach a shelter.
questions.explanation: Weather satellites help people see cyclones coming. An early warning gives families time to move to a cyclone shelter.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Raju makes a model of the solar system with eight balls of the same size. What can his model **not** show well?
options: how big each planet really is
that the Sun is in the middle
questions.explanation: His model shows the order and the number of planets, but the real planets are very different sizes (Jupiter is the biggest). Models also cannot show the huge distances.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: In the simulation, what does the Moon do while the Earth moves?

sim.task: Open Gravity and Orbits. Choose Sun, Earth and Moon, then press play. Watch the Moon for a while. You can tick the box that shows the paths.

options: It stays still in the middle.
It travels around the Sun only.
questions.explanation: The Moon orbits the Earth. At the same time, the Earth and Moon travel together around the Sun.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: In the simulation, the Earth goes once around the Sun in one year.

sim.task: Open Gravity and Orbits. Choose Sun and Earth, then press play. Watch the clock until the Earth has gone once around the Sun.

questions.explanation: The clock in the simulation shows that one orbit of the Earth around the Sun takes about one year.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: In the simulation, you turn gravity off while the Earth is moving. What happens to the Earth?

sim.task: Open Gravity and Orbits. Choose Sun and Earth, then press play. While the Earth is going round, turn gravity off and watch what happens.

options: It keeps going round in a circle.
It moves off in a straight line.
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls the Earth towards the Sun and bends its path into an orbit. With no gravity, nothing pulls it, so it moves off in a straight line.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: In 1610 Galileo saw four moons going around Jupiter. Why did this help Copernicus's idea?
options: It showed that Jupiter is the biggest planet.
It showed that the Sun is a star.
It showed that the Moon makes its own light.
It showed that not everything goes around the Earth.
questions.explanation: Copernicus said the planets go around the Sun. If four moons go around Jupiter, then Earth is not the centre of everything, which supported his idea.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Mina says, "The Sun is a planet because it is big and round." What is the best correction?
options: The Sun is a planet because the Earth orbits it.
The Sun is a moon because it is very hot.
The Sun is a star that makes its own light.
The Sun is a meteor because it is bright.
questions.explanation: A star is a ball of hot, glowing gas that makes its own light. The planets, including Earth, travel around our star, the Sun.

questions.title: The Solar System
questions.stem: Why do you think there is life on Earth but not on Mercury?
questions.model_answer: Earth has water, air and the right temperature. Mercury is too hot by day, too cold by night, and has no air.
questions.explanation: Living things need water, air and a suitable temperature. Earth has all three. Mercury is very hot in the day, very cold at night, and has almost no air.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Why do we have day and night?
options: The Sun goes around the Earth.
The Moon pushes the Sun away.
questions.explanation: The Earth spins (rotates) once every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day and the side facing away has night. The Sun does not really move around us.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: The Earth spins once every ___ hours. The Earth goes around the ___ once a year.
questions.explanation: One spin takes 24 hours, which gives us day and night. One trip around the Sun takes a year.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: The Sun moves around the Earth every day.
questions.explanation: The Earth spins, so the Sun only seems to move across the sky from east to west.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: A shadow stick has its shortest shadow at midday.
questions.explanation: At midday the Sun is highest in the sky, so the shadow is shortest. It is long in the morning and long again in the evening.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Put the phases of the Moon in order, starting at the new moon.
sequence: new moon
waxing crescent
first quarter
waxing gibbous
full moon
waning gibbous
last quarter
questions.explanation: The Moon goes from new moon to full moon as more of its lit side comes into view, then shrinks again through the waning phases.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: the imaginary line the Earth spins around
the shape of the lit part of the Moon we see
the sea going up and down each day
questions.explanation: The Earth rotates on its axis and orbits the Sun. A phase is the Moon's shape and a tide is the rise and fall of the sea.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: How do the seasons affect living things? Choose all that are right.
options: Farmers plant crops at the right season.
Some birds fly to Bangladesh in winter.
Trees grow new leaves in spring.
The Moon grows bigger in summer.
The Earth stops spinning in the rainy season.
questions.explanation: People, animals and plants all follow the seasons. The Moon's shape and the Earth's spin do not depend on the season.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.subskill: Movements of the Earth and Moon
questions.stem: Sort each event by the movement that causes it.
items: the Sun seeming to rise in the east
questions.explanation: The spin of the Earth gives day and night. The Earth's trip around the Sun (with its tilt) gives the year and the seasons. The Moon's trip around the Earth gives the phases.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: When it is day in Bangladesh, it is night in America. Why?
questions.model_answer: Bangladesh faces the Sun while America is on the other side of the spinning Earth, facing away from the Sun.
questions.explanation: The Earth is a ball, so the Sun lights only half of it at a time. When Bangladesh faces the Sun it has day while the far side has night.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: It is hotter in summer because the Sun is higher in the sky, so its light is stronger.
questions.explanation: In summer our part of the Earth leans towards the Sun. The Sun is high, the light is strong and the weather is warmer.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: The Moon travels around the Earth about once a month.
questions.explanation: The Moon orbits the Earth in about a month. As it moves, we see different amounts of its lit side, which are the phases.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: The Moon has no light of its own. It ___ sunlight.
questions.explanation: We see the Moon because sunlight bounces off it. The part we see lit changes as the Moon moves round the Earth.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Look at the stick and its shadow at three times of the day. When is the shadow shortest?
questions.image_alt: A stick and its shadow in the morning, at midday and in the evening as the Sun moves across the sky.
questions.explanation: At midday the Sun is at its highest, so the shadow is shortest. When the Sun is low in the morning and evening the shadow is long.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Look at the picture of the Earth and the Sun. Which part of the Earth has daytime?
questions.image_alt: The Sun lighting one half of the spinning Earth: day on the side facing the Sun and night on the other side.
options: the side facing away from the Sun
questions.explanation: The Sun lights the side of the Earth that faces it, so that side has day. The side facing away is in the dark, so it has night.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: The Earth is tilted. When the top half of the Earth leans towards the Sun, what season does that half have?
questions.image_alt: The tilted Earth at different places in its orbit around the Sun.
questions.explanation: Leaning towards the Sun means the Sun is higher and its light is stronger, so that half has summer. Six months later it leans away and has winter.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Which number shows the full moon?
questions.image_alt: Eight shapes of the Moon numbered 1 to 8 in order through a month.
questions.explanation: Number 5 is the full moon, when the whole lit side faces us. Number 1 is the new moon, when we cannot see the lit side at all.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Match each number in the picture to its Moon phase.
questions.image_alt: Eight shapes of the Moon numbered 1 to 8 in order through a month.
questions.explanation: The phases go in order: 1 new moon, 2 waxing crescent, 3 first quarter, 4 waxing gibbous, 5 full moon, 6 waning gibbous, 7 last quarter, 8 waning crescent.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Number 2 is a waxing crescent. This thin Moon will look bigger on the next few nights.
questions.image_alt: Eight shapes of the Moon numbered 1 to 8 in order through a month.
questions.explanation: "Waxing" means growing. After the crescent comes the first quarter, then the bigger gibbous Moon, and then the full moon.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Rafi's father is a fisher on the coast. Why does he watch the Moon?
options: The Moon makes the wind blow.
questions.explanation: The Moon's pull makes the tides rise and fall. At full moon and new moon the tides are very high and very low, so fishers plan when to go out and come in.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Families look for the thin new crescent moon. What does it tell them?
options: A new Islamic month has begun.
questions.explanation: The Islamic months begin when the new crescent moon is seen, so it also tells people when Eid will be celebrated.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Why do farmers in Bangladesh plant different crops in different seasons?
options: The Moon tells crops when to grow.
The Earth stops spinning in some seasons.
The weather changes through the year.
questions.explanation: Seasons bring different weather, such as heat, rain or cooler dry days. Farmers pick the crops that grow best in each one.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: At 8 am Imran's school shadow stick has a long shadow pointing west. Where will its shadow point at 4 pm?
questions.explanation: In the morning the Sun is in the east, so the shadow points west. In the afternoon the Sun is in the west, so the shadow points east and is long again.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.subskill: Movements of the Earth and Moon
questions.stem: In the simulation, the Earth stays still while the Sun goes around it.

sim.task: Open Gravity and Orbits. Choose Sun and Earth, then press play. Watch the clock until the Earth has made one trip around the Sun.

questions.explanation: The Earth is the one that moves: it goes around the Sun once a year, which the clock in the simulation shows. The Sun only seems to move across our sky because the Earth spins.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.subskill: Movements of the Earth and Moon
questions.stem: In the simulation, what does the Moon go around?

sim.task: Open Gravity and Orbits. Choose Sun, Earth and Moon, press play and tick the box that shows the paths. Watch where the Moon goes.

questions.explanation: The Moon orbits the Earth about once a month, while the Earth and Moon travel together around the Sun.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Class 3A measured a shadow stick: 8 am 80 cm, 10 am 40 cm, 12 noon 15 cm, 2 pm 35 cm, 4 pm 75 cm. What is the best prediction for 5 pm?
questions.explanation: As the Sun sinks lower in the evening, the shadow gets longer. At 4 pm it was 75 cm, so at 5 pm it should be longer than that.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Priya says, "It is summer because the Earth moves closer to the Sun." What is the best correction?
options: The Earth spins faster in summer.
The Earth is tilted, so in summer our part leans towards the Sun.
The Moon is brighter in summer.
The Sun moves nearer in summer.
questions.explanation: Seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth as it goes around the Sun. When we lean towards the Sun it is high in the sky and its light is stronger.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Explain how the spinning Earth makes the Sun seem to move across the sky from east to west.
questions.model_answer: The Earth spins, so the Sun only seems to move. It looks as if it rises in the east and sets in the west.
questions.explanation: It is the Earth that turns, not the Sun. As our part of the Earth turns towards the Sun we see it rise in the east, and as it turns away we see it set in the west.

questions.title: Day, Night, Seasons and the Moon
questions.stem: Which of these can people predict from patterns in the sky? Choose all that are right.
