options: The Sun will rise in the east tomorrow.
The Moon will pass through its phases again in about a month.
Summer will come again next year.
Exactly how much rain will fall next Tuesday.
questions.explanation: The spin of the Earth, the Moon's orbit and the Earth's orbit repeat in regular patterns, so we can predict them. Exact rainfall depends on changing weather.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: ___ is rotted plant waste that makes soil rich.
questions.explanation: Compost is made when plant waste such as peels and leaves rots. It adds goodness to the soil.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Match each of the three Rs to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Reduce means use less, reuse means use things again, and recycle means turn old things into new ones.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Sort each waste into solid, liquid or gas.
questions.explanation: Food scraps and plastic are solids. Dirty water is a liquid. Smoke and the carbon dioxide we breathe out are gases.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Which of these can be composted? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Plant and food waste rots and becomes compost. Plastic and metal do not rot, so they do not belong in a compost pit.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: A plastic bag buried in the soil will rot away within a few weeks.
questions.explanation: Plastic does not rot. A plastic bag buried for four weeks shows no change, so it stays in the environment for a very long time.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: The oxygen that plants release is a gas waste that is useful to us.
questions.explanation: Plants give out oxygen as a waste gas, and we need it to breathe. Not all waste is harmful.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a community makes compost.
sequence: Workers collect food and vegetable waste from homes.
The waste is piled in boxes at a compost plant.
Worms and microbes break the waste down.
After about two months it becomes dark, crumbly compost.
Farmers and gardeners use the compost on their soil.
questions.explanation: Food waste rots easily, so decomposers such as worms and microbes turn it into compost. Less rubbish goes to the dump and farmers get good soil.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Which is an example of **reusing**?
options: giving old paper to the bhangari collector
using an old jar as a pencil pot
questions.explanation: Reuse means using something again, so a jar can become a pencil pot. Giving paper to a collector is recycling, buying less packaging is reducing, and peels make compost.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Taking a cloth bag to the shop is an example of…
questions.explanation: A cloth bag can be used many times, so you use fewer plastic bags. Using less is called reducing.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: How can plastic bags cause floods in a city?
questions.model_answer: They block the drains, so rain water cannot flow away.
questions.explanation: Plastic bags do not rot. They collect in drains and stop rain water flowing away, so the streets flood.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Why is compost good for a garden?
options: It makes the soil hard like a brick.
It stops rain from falling on plants.
It keeps all the worms away.
It makes soil rich for plants.
questions.explanation: Compost adds goodness to the soil, so plants get what they need to grow well.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Rubbish heaps attract rats and flies that can spread disease.
questions.explanation: Rats and flies live and feed on rubbish. They can carry germs, so piles of waste can make people ill.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: To reduce is to use ___. To reuse is to use things ___.
questions.explanation: Reduce means use less. Reuse means use the same thing again instead of throwing it away.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Animals breathe out a waste gas called ___.
questions.explanation: Animals breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. Plants use carbon dioxide to make their food.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Dirty water from factories can pollute rivers like the Buriganga.
questions.explanation: Factory waste water often carries chemicals. When it flows into a river it pollutes the water and harms fish and the people who use the river.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into compost, recycle or reuse.
questions.explanation: Peels and leaves rot into compost. Paper and metal cans can be made into new things. A cloth bag and old clothes can be used again.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Which picture shows waste that can be composted?
questions.explanation: A banana peel is plant waste. It rots and turns into compost. Plastic, metal and glass do not rot.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Which picture shows a gas waste from vehicles?
questions.explanation: Exhaust fumes are gas waste. Spilled oil is a liquid, and a bottle and a banana peel are solids.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Match each picture to the kind of waste it shows.
questions.explanation: A bottle is a solid, oil is a liquid and smoke is a gas. Factories and vehicles make all three kinds of waste.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Which picture shows a good way to reduce waste when shopping?
questions.explanation: A cloth bag can be used again and again, so you need fewer plastic bags. Lots of packaging and new bottles make more waste.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: After heavy rain a street in Dhaka floods because plastic bags block the drain. What is the best long-term fix?
options: Use fewer plastic bags and bin used ones.
Burn the bags at the side of the street.
Throw the bags into the river instead.
Wait for the rain to stop falling.
questions.explanation: Using fewer bags and binning the rest stops plastic reaching drains. Burning makes smoke, and rivers are polluted by plastic too.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Mina's family has vegetable peels every day. What is the best thing to do with them?
options: Put them in a compost pit.
Put them with the plastic for recycling.
questions.explanation: Vegetable peels rot and become compost, which makes soil rich for plants. Rivers and the air should not be polluted.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Lina's family wants to give things to the bhangari collector for recycling. Which can they give? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Paper, metal and some plastic can be made into new things. Banana peels are best for compost.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Arif's neighbour burns a pile of rubbish behind the house. What is the problem?
options: The smoke makes the air unhealthy.
The fire makes the rubbish disappear safely.
The ashes will turn into compost.
questions.explanation: Smoke from burning rubbish is gas waste. It makes the air unhealthy to breathe, so it is better to compost, reuse or recycle.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Class 3B buried four things for four weeks. Banana peel: mostly gone. Paper: soft and falling apart. Plastic bag: no change. Metal bottle cap: no change, a little rust. Which conclusion is best?
options: Everything rots completely in four weeks.
Metal rots faster than paper does in soil.
Plant waste rots; plastic and metal do not.
Plastic bags rot faster than banana peels do.
questions.explanation: The banana peel and the paper came from plants, and decomposers broke them down. Plastic and metal showed no change, so they stay in the environment for a very long time.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Why is a plastic bag in a river a bigger problem than a banana peel?
questions.model_answer: Plastic does not rot, so it stays for a very long time and can harm fish and turtles. A banana peel rots away.
questions.explanation: A banana peel rots and becomes part of the soil. Plastic does not rot, so it keeps polluting and can harm animals or block drains.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: In an example neighbourhood, 40 families each make 2 kg of food waste a day. All of it is made into compost. How much food waste is kept out of the dump in 5 days?
questions.explanation: 40 families × 2 kg = 80 kg every day. Over 5 days that is 80 × 5 = 400 kg. 80 kg is only one day.

questions.title: Waste and Our World
questions.stem: Imran says, "Smoke from a fire is not waste because it just disappears into the air." What is the best reply?
options: Smoke is useful waste, just like the oxygen from plants.
Smoke is solid waste, so it can be recycled easily.
Smoke is only waste if you can see it clearly.
Smoke is gas waste, and it makes the air unhealthy.
questions.explanation: Smoke does not disappear: it spreads through the air and can harm our breathing. Smoke from fires, vehicles and factories is gas waste.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: A **property** of a material tells us…
questions.explanation: A property describes what a material is like, for example hard, shiny or waterproof. Every material has its own properties.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Match each property word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: These property words help us describe materials. A towel is absorbent, a raincoat is waterproof and a window is transparent.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Opposite words: shiny and ___; flexible and ___.
questions.explanation: A shiny material reflects light, so its opposite is dull. A flexible material bends easily, so its opposite is stiff.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: All metals are attracted by a magnet.
questions.explanation: A magnet attracts iron and steel (and a few others such as nickel). Aluminium, copper, gold and silver are metals that a magnet does not attract.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Sort these materials into hard and soft.
questions.explanation: Hard materials do not dent when you press them. Soft materials squash easily.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: A magnet attracts things made of ___ and steel.
questions.explanation: Magnetic materials are iron and steel. Wood, plastic and copper are not magnetic.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: A magnet is held near each object. Which objects will it pull? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Iron and steel are magnetic, so the nail, the paper clip and the pin are pulled. Aluminium and plastic are not magnetic.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Glass is used for windows because it is…
questions.explanation: Glass is transparent, so light comes in and we can see out. Wood is opaque, so it would block the light.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: A paper umbrella would be a good idea for the monsoon.
questions.explanation: Paper is absorbent and weak. It would get soggy and tear in the rain. An umbrella needs a waterproof material.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Put the steps of a fair test in order to find which material soaks up the most water.
sequence: Cut a square of the same size from each material.
Pour the same amount of water into each dish.
Put one square into each dish for one minute.
Lift the squares out and measure the water left in each dish.
Work out how much water each material soaked up.
questions.explanation: A fair test keeps everything the same (size, water, time) except the material. The water left tells you how much was soaked up.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Why is a window made of glass and not wood?
questions.model_answer: Glass is transparent, so light comes in and we can see through it. Wood is opaque and blocks the light.
questions.explanation: Windows must let light in, so they need a transparent material. Wood is opaque: you cannot see through it.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Jute is used to make sacks and rope because the fibres are…
questions.explanation: Jute fibres are strong and flexible, so they can be twisted into rope and woven into sacks and bags.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: A material that soaks up water is ___. A material that keeps water out is ___.
questions.explanation: A towel is absorbent, so it soaks up water. A plastic raincoat is waterproof, so water stays outside.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Which picture shows something **transparent**?
questions.explanation: You can see through the glass in a window, so it is transparent. A door, a brick and a log are opaque: you cannot see through them.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: A magnet is held over these pictures. Which one will it pick up?
questions.explanation: A paper clip is made of steel, and steel is magnetic. Feathers, plastic and wood are not magnetic.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Match each picture to the material it is mostly made of.
questions.explanation: Everyday objects are made from materials such as clay, glass, paper, cloth and metal.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Sort these things into magnetic and not magnetic.
questions.explanation: Paper clips, safety pins and sewing needles are made of steel, so a magnet attracts them. Plastic, feathers, wood and glass are not magnetic.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Which picture shows something that is both **hard** and **opaque**?
questions.explanation: A brick is hard and you cannot see through it. A sponge and yarn are soft, and a window is hard but transparent.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Mina is going to the bazar. She wants a strong bag that rots away safely when it is thrown out. Which bag should she take?
options: a bag made of cotton wool
questions.explanation: Jute is strong and rots away in the soil. A thin plastic bag stays for hundreds of years and can block drains.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: It is the monsoon. Anika needs a coat for the walk to school. Which material is best for the outside of the coat?
questions.explanation: A raincoat must keep water out, so its outer layer must be waterproof. Wool, paper and towel cloth soak up water.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Imran drops a steel needle into a pile of sand. What is the quickest way to find it?
options: Wave a plastic ruler over the sand.
Move a magnet over the sand.
Shine a torch on the sand.
questions.explanation: Steel is magnetic, so the needle jumps to the magnet. Sand is not magnetic and stays behind.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: A pot for cooking rice on a stove needs the right material. Which properties does the material need? Choose all that are right.
options: does not melt on a stove
questions.explanation: A cooking pot must be strong and must not melt on the stove. An absorbent or easily broken pot would be no use.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Farmers in Bangladesh store rice in jute sacks. Jute is a good material for sacks because the fibres are strong.
questions.explanation: Strong fibres do not tear easily, so jute sacks can hold heavy rice and be used again and again.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Class 3A put a 10 cm square of each material into 50 ml of water for one minute. Water left in the dish: cotton towel 20 ml, paper towel 30 ml, newspaper 40 ml, plastic 50 ml. Which statement is correct?
options: The plastic soaked up the most: 50 ml.
The paper towel soaked up more than the cotton towel.
The cotton towel soaked up the most: 30 ml.
questions.explanation: Water soaked up = 50 ml minus water left. Cotton towel 30 ml, paper towel 20 ml, newspaper 10 ml, plastic 0 ml. The plastic left all 50 ml behind, so it soaked up nothing.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Lina tests which cloth soaks up the most water. She puts a 10 cm square of cotton in 50 ml of water and a 20 cm square of wool in 100 ml of water. Why is this not a fair test?
options: She changed the size of the cloth and the amount of water, not only the material.
She should have used only one cloth in the whole test.
She used cloth instead of paper in the test.
She should have used no water in the test.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only one thing changes (here the material). Size, amount of water and time must stay the same.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Aisha says: "A coin is made of metal, so a magnet will always pick it up." Aisha is right.
questions.explanation: Some coins contain steel and stick to a magnet, but others are made of metals that are not magnetic. You must test each one.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: A builder needs a material for a footbridge over a canal. Which properties must it have? Give two.
questions.model_answer: It must be strong and stiff, and waterproof or not rot or rust in water.
questions.explanation: A bridge carries heavy loads, so it must be strong and stiff. It also stays outdoors in rain, so it must not rot or rust easily.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.stem: Four things are tested with a magnet. Which one is the odd one out?
questions.explanation: The nail, the pin and the paper clip are made of iron or steel, so a magnet attracts them. Aluminium is not magnetic.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: All sounds are made when something…
questions.explanation: Every sound starts with a vibration: something shaking back and forth very fast, like a drum skin or a guitar string.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Match each instrument to the part that vibrates.
pairs: the voice box in your throat
questions.explanation: Hitting, plucking and blowing all make a part of the instrument vibrate. When you speak, your voice box vibrates.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Sound can travel through water.
questions.explanation: Sound travels through gases (air), liquids (water) and solids. Whales and dolphins hear each other under water.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Astronauts can talk to each other in empty space without radios, because sound travels everywhere.
questions.explanation: Sound needs particles to pass the vibrations along. Space is almost empty, so sound cannot travel there. Astronauts use radios.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: We measure how loud a sound is in ___, using a sound level ___.
questions.explanation: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB) with a sound level meter. Many mobile phones have a sound meter app.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Which materials would be good at blocking sound? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Soft, thick materials such as curtains, foam and wool soak up sound vibrations. Thin, hard materials like foil and glass let much more sound through.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Sort these into higher pitch or lower pitch.
questions.explanation: Short, thin, tight and small things vibrate faster and make higher notes. Long, loose and big things vibrate slower and make lower notes.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how you hear a school bell.
sequence: The bell is hit and vibrates.
The air next to the bell vibrates.
The vibrations travel through the air.
The vibrations reach your ear.
Your brain tells you it is a bell.
questions.explanation: The vibrating bell makes the air vibrate. The vibration passes from particle to particle until it reaches your ear, and your brain makes sense of it.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: **Pitch** tells us how…
options: high or low a sound is
loud or quiet a sound is
questions.explanation: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. Loudness (volume) is a different thing: a high sound can be loud or quiet.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Put your ear on a desk while a friend taps the other end. Why do you hear the tap clearly?
questions.model_answer: Sound travels well through solids like the wooden desk, so the vibrations reach your ear clearly.
questions.explanation: Particles in a solid are close together, so they pass vibrations along very well. Sound travels better through solids than through air.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Materials that stop sound from travelling through them are called sound ___.
questions.explanation: Sound insulation, like foam or thick cloth, soaks up vibrations so less sound gets through.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: An ektara player presses her finger on the string to make it shorter. What happens to the note?
questions.explanation: A shorter string vibrates faster, so the pitch goes up. Plucking harder would make it louder, not higher.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: The bottles are tapped with a spoon. Which bottle makes the **highest** note?
questions.image_alt: Four glass bottles A to D. A has the least water and D has the most.
questions.explanation: When you tap a bottle, the glass and water vibrate. Less water means less to shake, so it vibrates faster: bottle A gives the highest note.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Look at the four sound pictures. Which one shows a **loud, high** sound?
questions.image_alt: Four wave drawings A to D: tall wide waves, short wide waves, tall close waves and short close waves.
questions.explanation: Taller waves mean a louder sound. Waves closer together mean a higher pitch. C has tall, close waves: loud and high.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Use the decibel scale. Which sound could damage your hearing if you listened for a long time?
questions.image_alt: A decibel scale from 0 to 140 with leaves 20, birds 40, talking 60, traffic 80, loud music 100 and a plane 120 dB. Above 85 dB is shaded.
questions.explanation: Sounds above about 85 dB can damage hearing. Loud music is about 100 dB, so it is in the danger zone.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Match each picture to how it makes a sound.
questions.explanation: Hitting, plucking, blowing and shaking are different ways of making something vibrate.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Two children made this string telephone. What must they do to make it work best?
questions.image_alt: Two cups joined by a long string.
options: Use a very short string with a knot in it.
Hold the string with their fingers in the middle.
questions.explanation: Vibrations travel along a tight string. A loose string, or fingers touching it, stops the vibrations.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: A family lives next to a busy road in Dhaka. The baby cannot sleep because of the noise. What is the best thing to try first?
options: Hang thick curtains and put a rug on the floor.
Put a metal sheet on the bed.
questions.explanation: Thick, soft materials such as curtains and rugs absorb sound. Opening windows lets more noise in, and paint or metal do not soak up sound.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Rafi works in a factory with loud machines all day. Which advice is the most important for his health?
questions.explanation: Loud sounds above about 85 dB, heard for a long time, can damage hearing. Ear defenders block the sound.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Mitu says: 'The road outside the hospital is a silent zone, so drivers must not honk their horns.' Is this a sensible rule?
questions.explanation: Sick people need rest, and loud horns can harm hearing and sleep. Silent zones near hospitals and schools protect people from noise.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Your class wants a quiet reading corner. Which changes would help? Choose all that are right.
options: put cushions and a soft rug there
hang a cloth curtain around it
put it next to the noisy door
line one wall with egg boxes or foam
add a metal bin to drum on
questions.explanation: Soft, thick, bumpy materials absorb sound. Being next to the door, or adding something to bang, makes the corner noisier.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the sound when you move the **frequency** slider up?

sim.task: Open Sound Waves. Turn on the sound so you can hear the speaker. Move the frequency slider from low to high and listen. Watch the waves.

options: The sound gets louder and the waves get taller.
The pitch gets higher and the waves get closer together.
questions.explanation: Frequency is how many vibrations happen each second. More vibrations each second means a higher pitch, so the waves are drawn closer together.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens when you move the **amplitude** slider up?

sim.task: Open Sound Waves. Keep the frequency the same. Move the amplitude slider from low to high and listen.

questions.explanation: Amplitude is how big the vibrations are. Bigger vibrations make a louder sound, but the pitch stays the same.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: In the simulation, when the air is removed from around the speaker, the sound becomes quieter.

sim.task: Open Sound Waves and choose the Air Pressure screen. Turn the sound on, then remove the air from around the speaker and listen.

questions.explanation: Sound needs particles to travel. With less air around the speaker, there are fewer particles to pass on the vibrations, so less sound reaches you.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: In a thunderstorm you see the lightning before you hear the thunder, although both happen at the same time. What does this tell you?
options: Your ears work more slowly than your eyes.
The thunder happens later than the lightning.
Light travels much faster than sound.
questions.explanation: Light reaches you almost instantly, but sound travels much more slowly through air. The bigger the gap, the further away the storm.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Class 3C tested materials around a ringing alarm clock: none 70 dB, foil 66 dB, newspaper 60 dB, towel 50 dB, foam 45 dB. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: All the materials blocked the same amount.
Shiny materials blocked the most sound.
Soft, thick materials blocked the most sound.
Paper is the best sound insulator.
questions.explanation: Foam and the towel (soft, thick) gave the lowest readings. Foil (shiny, thin) blocked the least. The data support 'soft, thick materials block most sound'.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: A guitar has six strings of the same length. The thickest string makes the lowest note. Explain why.
questions.model_answer: A thicker string is heavier, so it vibrates more slowly, and slower vibrations make a lower pitch.
questions.explanation: The thicker the string, the more slowly it vibrates. Fewer vibrations each second make a lower note.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Which word means how loud a sound is?
questions.explanation: Volume (loudness) is how loud or quiet a sound is. Pitch is how high or low it is.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Heat is a kind of ___ that makes things warmer.
questions.explanation: Heat is a kind of energy. When you rub your hands together, they get warm.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Which of these are sources of heat? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: The Sun, fire, electric heaters and light bulbs all give out heat. An ice cube is cold: it takes in heat and melts.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Match each thing to its temperature.
questions.explanation: Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius. Ice melts at 0 °C, our body is about 37 °C and water boils at 100 °C.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: We measure temperature in degrees ___ using a ___.
questions.explanation: Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius (°C) with a thermometer. The liquid inside rises when it gets warmer.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Is heat added or removed? Sort these changes.
items: wet clothes dry in the sun
questions.explanation: Melting, cooking and drying need heat to be added. Freezing, cooling and setting hard happen when heat is taken away.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Rafi stirs hot tea with a metal spoon. Put the steps in order to show how the heat reaches his fingers.
sequence: The hot tea heats the bottom of the spoon.
Heat travels up through the metal.
The handle of the spoon gets hot.
Rafi's fingers feel the heat.
questions.explanation: Heat travels through the solid metal from the hot end to the cold end. This is called conduction.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Heat always moves from…
questions.explanation: Heat always moves from hotter places to colder places. That is why a hot drink cools down and a cold drink warms up.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Match each way heat travels to what happens.
pairs: warm water or air rises and cool water or air sinks
questions.explanation: Conduction is for solids, convection is for liquids and gases that move, and radiation needs no material at all: it is how the Sun warms us.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Sort these into conductors and insulators of heat.
questions.explanation: Metals let heat through easily, so they are conductors. Wood, wool and plastic do not, so they are insulators.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: A woolly jumper keeps you warm because wool makes its own heat.
questions.explanation: Wool does not make heat. It is an insulator and traps air, so your body heat stays in.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Why do cooking pots have wooden or plastic handles?
questions.model_answer: Wood and plastic are insulators, so the handle does not get too hot to hold.
questions.explanation: The pot is metal, which conducts heat. A wooden or plastic handle is an insulator, so you can hold it without burning your hand.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Look at the thermometers. Which one could show the temperature of a healthy person?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C reading 12 °C, 37 °C and 48 °C.
questions.explanation: A healthy body is about 37 °C, so thermometer B is the one. A (12 °C) is much too cold and C (48 °C) is much too hot.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: What temperature does thermometer C show?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C reading 5 °C, 25 °C and 40 °C.
questions.explanation: Thermometer C reads 40 °C. Thermometer A reads 5 °C and B reads 25 °C.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Which picture shows heat travelling through a solid?
questions.image_alt: Three pictures: A a spoon in a hot drink, B a pot of water over a flame with arrows, C the Sun warming a hand.
questions.explanation: In picture A the heat travels along the metal spoon: that is conduction. B shows convection in water and C shows radiation from the Sun.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Sort these pictures into things that give out heat and things that do not.
questions.explanation: The Sun, fire, light bulbs and candles are sources of heat. Ice, snow and icebergs are cold.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: The four cups hold the same amount of hot water. Only one thing is different. What is being changed in this investigation?
questions.image_alt: Four cups of hot water: one with no cover and others wrapped in newspaper, wool and foil.
questions.explanation: The cups are the same and have the same hot water. Only the cover is different (none, newspaper, wool or foil), so the test finds out which cover keeps heat in best.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Priya touches a hot pan by accident and gets a small burn on her finger. What should she do first?
options: Put it near the fire to dry it and carry on cooking.
Hold it under clean running water for 20 minutes and tell an adult.
Wrap it in a dry cloth and tell nobody about it.
Rub it hard with a rough cloth and wait.
questions.explanation: Cool a burn under clean running water for 20 minutes and tell an adult. Hiding a burn or rubbing it can make it worse.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: On a cold winter night in the north of Bangladesh, Nadia wants to stay warm safely. Which is the best choice?
options: Sleep on the cold floor under a thin sheet.
Wear one thin shirt and open the window.
Sleep very close to the open fire.
Wear warm layers and use a thick quilt.
questions.explanation: Layers and a quilt trap air, which is an insulator, so body heat stays in. Sleeping close to an open fire is dangerous.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Tuli's family sits near a small open fire on a cold night. Which rules are safe? Choose all that are right.
options: Tie back loose clothes such as an orna.
Go to sleep and leave the fire burning.
Hang a shawl over the fire to dry it.
questions.explanation: Sit away from the fire, tie back loose clothes and keep water or sand nearby. Never leave a fire alone or put cloth near it.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Joy's clothes catch fire. Put the safe steps in order.
sequence: Stop moving.
Drop to the ground.
Roll over to put out the flames.
questions.explanation: Stop, drop and roll. Running makes the flames bigger and rolling smothers them.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: It is safe to touch the flat plate of an electric iron to check whether it is hot.
questions.explanation: Irons, stoves, hot oil and steam can burn you. Never touch them to test them.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the thermometer reading in the water?

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Intro screen. Drag the beaker of water onto the stand above the burner and drag a thermometer into the water. Slide the burner control up to heat the water and watch the thermometer for a minute.

questions.explanation: The burner adds heat to the water, so the water gets hotter and the thermometer reading rises.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the two thermometers?

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Intro screen. Drag one thermometer onto the iron block and one onto the brick block. Heat the iron block with the burner, then move it so that it touches the cooler brick block. Watch both thermometers.

options: The iron's reading goes down and the brick's reading goes up.
questions.explanation: Heat moves from the hotter iron block to the cooler brick block. The iron loses heat and cools, and the brick gains heat and warms, until they are the same temperature.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: In the simulation, when the burner is set to the blue cooling side under the water, the temperature of the water goes down.

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Intro screen. Put the beaker of water on the stand above the burner and drag a thermometer into the water. Slide the burner control to the blue cooling side and watch the thermometer for a minute.

questions.explanation: Cooling takes heat away from the water, so its temperature falls.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Class 3A filled four cups with hot water at 80 °C and covered three of them. After 20 minutes the temperatures were: no cover 45 °C, newspaper 52 °C, wool 60 °C, foil 55 °C. Which statement is best supported?
options: Foil was the best insulator of the four.
Newspaper was a better insulator than wool.
The cup with no cover kept the most heat.
Wool was the best insulator of the four.
questions.explanation: The hottest water after 20 minutes (60 °C) was in the wool cup, so wool let the least heat escape. The cup with no cover cooled the most (45 °C).

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Raju wraps one cold bottle of water in a woollen scarf and leaves another bottle unwrapped on the table. After an hour the unwrapped bottle is warmer. Why?
options: Wool gives out cold and chills the bottle.
Wool is a good conductor, so it carried heat away.
Wool is an insulator, so it slowed the heat moving into the wrapped bottle.
The unwrapped bottle was heavier than the other.
questions.explanation: Insulators slow heat down in both directions: they keep warm things warm and cold things cold. Wool does not give out cold.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: Design a box to keep a lunch of hot rice warm. Which materials would you use and why?
questions.model_answer: A metal tiffin box wrapped in wool or cloth and put in a plastic bag. These insulators trap the heat so the rice stays warm.
questions.explanation: To keep heat in, wrap the food in insulators such as wool, cloth or foam. Air trapped in these materials slows the heat escaping.

questions.title: Heat and Temperature
questions.stem: In an example experiment, a dot of wax is put on the end of four spoons. The other ends are put in the same hot water. The wax melts after 40 seconds on the aluminium spoon and 60 seconds on the steel spoon. After 5 minutes the wax on the wooden and plastic spoons has not melted. Which conclusion is best?
options: Wood and plastic are the best conductors.
Steel conducts heat faster than aluminium.
Metals are good conductors and wood and plastic are insulators.
All four spoons conduct heat equally well.
questions.explanation: Heat reached the wax fastest through aluminium, then steel, so metals conduct well. It did not reach the wax through wood or plastic, so they are insulators.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Match each part of a circuit to its job.
pairs: opens or closes a gap in the circuit
questions.explanation: A circuit needs a cell to push the electricity round, wires to carry it, and something to use it, such as a lamp or buzzer. A switch lets us turn it on and off.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: A lamp will light only if the circuit is a complete loop.
questions.explanation: Electricity can flow only if there is no gap. If the loop is complete, the lamp lights.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Electricity can flow only if the circuit is a complete ___.
questions.explanation: A circuit is a loop. Electricity flows from one end of the cell, through the wires and the lamp, and back to the other end.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show what happens when you close the switch in a working circuit.
sequence: The switch is closed.
The gap in the circuit is closed.
Electricity flows all the way round the loop.
The lamp lights.
questions.explanation: Closing the switch fills the gap. With a complete loop, electricity can flow round and the lamp lights.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: In the model of electric current, tiny particles in the wires…
options: are all used up by the lamp
fly out of the wires into the air
questions.explanation: In the model, the cell pushes the particles and they flow all the way round the loop, like children in a ring passing a ball. They are not used up.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Sort these objects into those a magnet attracts and those it does not.
questions.explanation: Magnets attract iron and steel. Aluminium, copper and plastic are not magnetic.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Will the magnets attract or repel? Sort these.
questions.explanation: Different poles attract. Two poles that are the same repel, which means they push apart.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Which materials does a magnet attract? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: A magnet attracts iron and steel. Aluminium and copper are metals that are not attracted, and plastic is not a metal at all.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Each magnet has two ends called ___: north and south.
questions.explanation: The two ends of a magnet are its poles, a north pole (N) and a south pole (S).

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Use the particle model to explain why the lamp goes out when you open the switch.
questions.model_answer: Opening the switch makes a gap, so the ring of particles is broken. The particles cannot flow round the circuit, so the lamp goes out.
questions.explanation: The particles can only flow round a complete loop, like children passing a ball in a ring. If the ring breaks, everything stops.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Look at the circuit. What will the lamp do?
questions.image_alt: A circuit with a cell, a lamp and a closed switch.
questions.explanation: The cell, wires, lamp and closed switch make a complete loop, so electricity flows and the lamp lights.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Look at the circuit. Why is the lamp off?
questions.image_alt: A circuit with a cell, a lamp and an open switch.
options: The lamp has been put in the circuit the wrong way round.
There are too many wires in the circuit.
The wires in the circuit are too short.
The open switch makes a gap in the loop.
questions.explanation: An open switch is a gap in the circuit. Electricity cannot flow across the gap, so the lamp stays off.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Compared with one lamp in a circuit with one cell, how bright are the two lamps in this picture?
questions.image_alt: A circuit with one cell and two lamps in a loop.
questions.explanation: The two lamps share the electricity from one cell, so each is dimmer than a single lamp would be.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Look at the bar magnets. What happens when two north poles face each other?
questions.image_alt: Bar magnets: north facing south attract; north facing north repel.
options: They stick and cannot be moved.
questions.explanation: Two poles that are the same repel each other. Different poles attract.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Sort these pictures into things that need electricity to work and things that do not.
questions.explanation: Fans, televisions, phones and light bulbs all use electricity. A bicycle, a candle, a broom and a hammer do not.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Rafi finds a loose wire sticking out of a wall socket. What is the safe thing to do?
options: Push it back into the socket with a pencil.
Pull it out of the socket with wet hands.
Cover it with a wet cloth and walk away.
Do not touch it and tell an adult.
questions.explanation: Mains electricity is very dangerous and can kill. Never touch sockets or wires, and never use wet hands. Tell an adult.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Raju's torch does not light. Which could be the reason? Choose all that are right.
options: A wire has come loose, leaving a gap.
questions.explanation: A torch needs a cell with electricity and a complete loop. A flat cell, an open switch or a gap all stop it working. Weight and colour make no difference.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: A scrapyard crane has a huge magnet to lift scrap. Which scrap can it lift?
questions.explanation: Iron is magnetic, so the crane magnet pulls it up. Aluminium, copper and plastic are not magnetic.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: A solar home system in a village has a solar panel, a battery, wires, switches and lamps. At night the battery lights the lamps.
questions.explanation: The solar panel charges the battery in the day. At night the battery sends electricity round the circuit to the lamps.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: In a solar home system, the solar panel turns ___ into electricity, which is stored in a ___.
questions.explanation: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity. The battery stores it so that families can use lamps at night without smoky kerosene lamps.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the bulb when you open the switch?

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit: DC. Drag a battery, a light bulb, a switch and some wires onto the board and join them in one loop with the switch closed, so the bulb is lit. Now click the switch to open it.

questions.explanation: Opening the switch makes a gap in the loop, so electricity stops flowing and the bulb goes out.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: In the simulation, which objects make the bulb light? Choose all that are right.

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit: DC and choose the Lab screen. Join a battery and a bulb with wires but leave a gap in the loop. Put each object in the gap one at a time: the paper clip, the coin, the eraser and the dollar bill. Watch the bulb.

questions.explanation: Metals such as the paper clip and coin let electricity through and complete the circuit. The eraser and the dollar bill do not.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the brightness of the bulbs when you add a second bulb in the same loop?

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit: DC. Build a loop with one battery and one bulb and look at how bright it is. Then add a second bulb in the same loop (in a line with the first) and compare.

options: They are dimmer than one bulb alone.
They are brighter than one bulb alone.
They stay the same as one bulb alone.
questions.explanation: The two bulbs share the electricity from one battery, so each is dimmer.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: In the simulation, when you flip the bar magnet over, the compass needle turns to point the opposite way.

sim.task: Open Magnet and Compass. Drag the compass close to one end of the bar magnet and see which way the needle points. Now flip the magnet over and watch the needle.

questions.explanation: A compass needle is a small magnet. When the poles of the bar magnet swap places, the needle swaps too.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: A circuit has one cell, a closed switch and two lamps joined in one loop. Both lamps are lit. Imran unscrews one lamp from its holder. What happens to the other lamp?
options: It gets brighter, because it now gets all the electricity.
It stays the same, because electricity goes round the gap.
It flickers for a moment, then stays lit.
It goes out too, because the loop is broken.
questions.explanation: Unscrewing a lamp makes a gap in the only loop. Electricity cannot flow anywhere, so the other lamp goes out too.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Class 3B hung paper clips in a chain from each magnet until no more would stick. Results: bar magnet 8, horseshoe magnet 12, ring magnet 5, fridge magnet 2. Which statement is correct?
options: The ring magnet held more clips than the bar magnet.
The horseshoe magnet held 4 more clips than the bar magnet.
The bar magnet was the strongest magnet.
questions.explanation: 12 minus 8 is 4, so the horseshoe held 4 more than the bar. The horseshoe held the most clips, so it was the strongest.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: Nadia's lamp does not light because there is a gap in a wire. Using a stronger cell will make it light.
questions.explanation: Electricity cannot cross a gap, however strong the cell is. She must close the gap to make a complete loop.

questions.title: Electricity and Magnets
questions.stem: How could you use a magnet to separate iron nails from sand?
questions.model_answer: Move a magnet through the mixture. The iron nails stick to the magnet and the sand stays behind.
questions.explanation: Iron is magnetic and sand is not. The magnet picks up the nails and leaves the sand.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: A simple machine is a tool that…
questions.explanation: A simple machine has few or no moving parts and makes work easier. It can let us use less force, change the direction of a force, or move something further or faster.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Which of these are simple machines? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Levers, ramps and pulleys are simple machines. Phones and televisions are complicated electrical devices.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: A lever is a bar that turns on a point called the ___.
questions.explanation: The fulcrum (pivot) is the point a lever turns on. The effort is your push or pull, and the load is the thing being moved.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Match each lever word to its meaning.
pairs: the push or pull you give
the point a lever turns on
questions.explanation: When you press a spoon under a tin lid, your push is the effort, the lid is the load and the rim of the tin is the fulcrum.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Sort these into levers, ramps, and pulleys or gears.
questions.explanation: Levers turn on a fulcrum. Ramps are slopes. Pulleys use a wheel and rope, and gears are wheels with teeth.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: A ramp lets you use less force, but you must move the load further.
questions.explanation: It is easier to push a heavy load up a ramp than to lift it straight up, but the path is longer.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Why is it easier to open a tin lid with a long spoon than with a coin?
options: The spoon is heavier, so the lid feels lighter to open.
The spoon is made of a different metal, so the lid is lighter.
The effort is further from the fulcrum, so less force is needed.
A coin has sharp edges, so it cannot touch the lid.
questions.explanation: The longer the handle, the further your push is from the fulcrum, and the less force you need. The lid does not get lighter.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a flag is raised with a pulley.
sequence: The flag is tied to the rope.
The rope goes over the pulley wheel at the top of the pole.
Someone pulls down on the rope.
The flag goes up the pole.
questions.explanation: A pulley is a wheel with a rope over it. Pulling down on the rope lifts the flag up.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: A pulley is a wheel with a ___ over it. Gears are wheels with ___ that turn each other.
questions.explanation: Pulleys lift buckets from wells and flags up poles. Gears, in bicycles, clocks and rice mills, turn each other with their teeth.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: How does a pulley help someone raise a flag?
questions.model_answer: Pulling down on the rope makes the flag go up, so the person can stay on the ground and pull in an easy direction.
questions.explanation: A pulley changes the direction of the force. Pulling down is easier than climbing the pole to push the flag up.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: A ramp makes a heavy load lighter.
questions.explanation: The load keeps the same weight. A ramp lets you move it a longer way with less force at a time.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Look at the see-saw lever. Which number shows the **fulcrum**?
questions.image_alt: A see-saw lever with three parts numbered: 1 effort, 2 fulcrum, 3 load.
questions.explanation: The fulcrum (pivot) is the point the see-saw turns on: number 2. Number 1 is the effort (push) and number 3 is the load.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Look at the six simple machines. Match each letter to its name.
questions.image_alt: Six simple machines lettered A to F: lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge and screw.
questions.explanation: A is a lever, B a pulley, C a wheel and axle, and D an inclined plane (ramp). E is a wedge and F is a screw.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: The handle of a hand tubewell is a lever. Which number shows the handle you push?
questions.image_alt: A hand tubewell: 1 handle, 2 pivot, 3 pump body, 4 spout, 5 pipe to underground water.
questions.explanation: Number 1 is the handle, which is the lever. Number 2 is the pivot (fulcrum). A long handle makes it easier to lift the water.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Lifting the box straight up needs 10 N. Pulling it up the ramp needs 4 N. What does the picture show?
questions.image_alt: Lifting a box straight up needs 10 N; pulling it up a ramp needs 4 N.
options: The ramp needs more force than lifting.
The ramp makes the box lighter.
The ramp needs the same force but is shorter.
The ramp needs less force but a longer path.
questions.explanation: The ramp lets you use less force (4 N instead of 10 N), but the box travels a longer way.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Match each picture to the simple machine it shows.
questions.explanation: Scissors are two levers joined at a pivot. A slide is a ramp. Gears are wheels with teeth. A wheel turns on an axle.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: The forcemeter shows ___ newtons (N).
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter reading 7 newtons.
questions.explanation: Read the pointer on the scale: it points to 7 N.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Nadia must put a heavy sack of rice onto a truck. Which way needs the least force?
options: Push it up a long, gentle ramp.
Push it up a short, steep ramp.
Lift it straight up by hand.
questions.explanation: A long, gentle ramp needs the least force. A short, steep ramp is hard work, and lifting straight up needs the most force.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: In many villages women husk rice with a long wooden dheki, which turns on a pivot. What kind of simple machine is a dheki?
questions.explanation: A dheki is a long beam that turns on a pivot. One end is stepped on and the other end lifts and thumps down, so it is a lever.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: A tubewell handle is a lever. Pumping the long handle takes less force than lifting the water straight up by hand.
questions.explanation: The long handle is a lever. The longer the handle, the less force you need to lift the water.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Imran must raise a heavy box into the back of a truck. Which things could help? Choose all that are right.
options: a long plank used as a ramp
a pulley and rope fixed above
a long bar used as a lever
questions.explanation: A ramp, a pulley and a lever are simple machines that make the job easier. Shaking the box or pushing with no tool does not help.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the plank when you remove the supports?

sim.task: Open Balancing Act and choose the Intro screen. Drag one brick onto the left side of the plank and an identical brick onto the right side at the same distance from the pivot. Then remove the supports under the plank.

questions.explanation: Two identical bricks at equal distances from the pivot pull down equally, so the plank balances.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: In the simulation, which side goes down?

sim.task: Open Balancing Act and choose the Intro screen. Put one brick on the left side of the plank, far from the pivot. Put an identical brick on the right side, close to the pivot. Then remove the supports under the plank.

options: The right side, where the brick is closer to the pivot.
Neither side, because the bricks weigh the same.
The left side, where the brick is further from the pivot.
questions.explanation: The two bricks weigh the same, but the one further from the pivot has a bigger turning effect, so the plank tips on that side.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: In the simulation, one brick on the left and two bricks on the right at the same distance from the pivot make the right side go down.

sim.task: Open Balancing Act and choose the Intro screen. Put one brick on the left side and two bricks on the right side, both at the same distance from the pivot. Then remove the supports under the plank.

questions.explanation: More weight at the same distance gives a bigger turning effect, so the heavier side goes down.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Class 3C pulled a toy truck up ramps with a forcemeter. Force needed: 10 cm ramp 3 N, 20 cm ramp 5 N, 30 cm ramp 7 N, lifting straight up 10 N. Which statement is correct?
options: The 30 cm ramp needed 3 N less than lifting straight up.
The 20 cm ramp needed more force than the 30 cm ramp.
Lifting straight up needed the least force.
questions.explanation: 10 N minus 7 N is 3 N. The lower the ramp, the less force is needed: 3 N, 5 N, 7 N and then 10 N for lifting straight up.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Rafi is heavier than his little sister Tuli. They want to balance on a see-saw. Where should Tuli sit?
options: closer to the middle than Rafi
the same distance from the middle as Rafi
on the same side as Rafi
further from the middle than Rafi
questions.explanation: A lighter person further from the pivot can balance a heavier person who sits closer to it.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: Design a machine to lift a bucket of sand to a first-floor window. Name the simple machines you use.
questions.model_answer: Fix a pulley above the window and put a rope over it. Tie the bucket to one end and pull down on the other end from the ground. A winding handle (wheel and axle) could make it easier.
questions.explanation: A pulley with a rope lets you stand on the ground and pull down to raise the load. Other simple machines can help too.

questions.title: Simple Machines
questions.stem: A steeper ramp needs less force than a gentle ramp to lift the same load.
questions.explanation: The gentler (lower) the ramp, the less force is needed. A steep ramp is closer to lifting the load straight up.
